note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Physics board exam 2024, Q.P. code 55/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Two figure-only alternatives (Q29(iv)(a) and Q30(iv)(b)) are left out; other figures are described in words. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A thin plastic rod is bent into a circular ring of radius R. It is uniformly charged with charge density λ. The magnitude of the electric field at its centre is :
questions.solution: By symmetry, the fields of diametrically opposite elements cancel, so E = 0 at the centre.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Ten capacitors, each of capacitance 1 μF, are connected in parallel to a source of 100 V. The total energy stored in the system is equal to :

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two cells are connected in parallel between points A and B with like terminals together: one branch has a 12 V cell in series with a 1 Ω resistor and the other has a 6 V cell in series with a 0.5 Ω resistor. The potential difference between points A and B is :
questions.solution: E_eq = (E₁/r₁ + E₂/r₂)/(1/r₁ + 1/r₂) = (12 + 12)/(1 + 2) = 8 V. With no external current, V_AB = 8 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A loop carrying a current I clockwise is placed in the x-y plane, in a uniform magnetic field directed along the z-axis. The tendency of the loop will be to :
questions.solution: The net force on a loop in a uniform field is zero. Taking B along +z, the force IL × B on each side of a clockwise loop points inwards, so the loop tends to shrink.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 10 cm long wire lies along the y-axis. It carries a current of 1.0 A in the positive y-direction. A magnetic field B = (5 mT) ĵ − (8 mT) k̂ exists in the region. The force on the wire is :

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A galvanometer of resistance G Ω is converted into an ammeter of range 0 to I A. If the current through the galvanometer is 0.1% of I A, the resistance of the ammeter is :
questions.solution: I_g = I/1000, so the shunt S = I_gG/(I − I_g) = G/999. Ammeter resistance = GS/(G + S) = G/1000.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The reactance of a capacitor of capacitance C connected to an ac source of frequency ω is X. If the capacitance of the capacitor is doubled and the frequency of the source is tripled, the reactance will become :
questions.solution: X = 1/(ωC). With 3ω and 2C: X′ = X/6.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In four regions I, II, III and IV, the electric fields are described as: Region I: Eₓ = E₀ sin(kz − ωt); Region II: Eₓ = E₀; Region III: Eₓ = E₀ sin kz; Region IV: Eₓ = E₀ cos kz. The displacement current will exist in the region :
questions.solution: Displacement current needs a time-varying field (dE/dt ≠ 0); only region I's field changes with time.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The transition of the electron that gives rise to the second spectral line of the Balmer series in the spectrum of the hydrogen atom corresponds to :
questions.solution: Balmer lines end on n = 2; the second line starts from n = 4.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Ge is doped with As. Due to doping,
options: the structure of Ge lattice is distorted.
the number of conduction electrons increases.
the number of conduction electrons decreases.
questions.solution: Arsenic is pentavalent; each atom donates a free electron, making n-type Ge.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: Two beams A and B, whose photon energies are 3.3 eV and 11.3 eV respectively, illuminate a metallic surface (work function 2.3 eV) successively. The ratio of maximum speed of electrons emitted due to beam A to that due to beam B is :
questions.solution: Kmax = 1 eV and 9 eV. v ∝ √K, so the ratio is √(1/9) = 1/3.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: The waves associated with a moving electron and a moving proton have the same wavelength λ. It implies that they have the same :
questions.solution: λ = h/p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text:
Assertion (A): In the photoelectric effect, the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons increases with increase in the intensity of the incident light.
Reason (R): Photoelectric current depends on the wavelength of the incident light.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: Kmax depends on frequency, not intensity, so A is false. The photocurrent depends on intensity, not wavelength (above threshold), so R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The mutual inductance between two coils is maximum when the coils are wound on each other.
Reason (R): The flux linkage between two coils is maximum when they are wound on each other.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: Winding one coil on the other gives the largest flux linkage, and M = NΦ/I, so R explains A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Two long parallel wires, freely suspended and connected in series to a battery, move apart.
Reason (R): Two wires carrying current in opposite directions repel each other.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: In series, the current flows out along one wire and back along the other, i.e. in opposite directions, so the wires repel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Plane and convex mirrors cannot produce real images under any circumstance.
Reason (R): A virtual image cannot serve as an object to produce a real image.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false and Reason (R) is also false.
questions.solution: Both mirrors give real images of virtual (converging) objects, so A is false. A virtual image can act as an object (as in a microscope's eyepiece forming images from the objective's image), so R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Find the temperature at which the resistance of a wire made of silver will be twice its resistance at 20 °C. Take 20 °C as the reference temperature and the temperature coefficient of resistance of silver at 20 °C = 4.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹.
questions.solution: R = R₀(1 + αΔT). 2 = 1 + 4 × 10⁻³ ΔT, so ΔT = 250 K and T = 270 °C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Monochromatic light of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz passes from air into a medium of refractive index 1.5. Find the wavelength of the light (i) reflected, and (ii) refracted at the interface of the two media.
questions.solution: (i) Reflected light stays in air: λ = c/ν = 3 × 10⁸/5 × 10¹⁴ = 600 nm. (ii) Refracted: λ/n = 600/1.5 = 400 nm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A plano-convex lens of focal length 16 cm is made of a material of refractive index 1.4. Calculate the radius of the curved surface of the lens.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm. Find the (i) position of the image formed and (ii) magnification of the image.
questions.solution: f = −20 cm, u = −30 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/20 + 1/30 = −1/60, so v = −60 cm (60 cm in front, real). m = −v/u = −2 (inverted, twice the size).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.text: Consider a neutron (mass m) of kinetic energy E and a photon of the same energy. Let λₙ and λₚ be the de Broglie wavelength of the neutron and the wavelength of the photon respectively. Obtain an expression for λₙ/λₚ.
questions.solution: λₙ = h/√(2mE) and λₚ = hc/E. So λₙ/λₚ = E/(c√(2mE)) = (1/c)√(E/(2m)).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Plot a graph showing the variation of current with voltage for the material GaAs. On the graph, mark the region where (a) resistance is negative, and (b) Ohm's law is obeyed.
questions.solution: The current rises linearly at first (Ohm's law region, near the origin), reaches a peak, then falls as voltage increases further (negative resistance region), and later rises again. (a) Negative resistance: the falling part after the peak. (b) Ohm's law: the initial straight-line part.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A cube of side 0.1 m is placed in a region where the electric field E = 500x î exists (x in metres, E in N C⁻¹). The cube's edges are parallel to the axes, with one face in the plane x = 0.1 m and the opposite face in the plane x = 0.2 m. Calculate (a) the flux passing through the cube, and (b) the charge within the cube.
questions.solution: (a) Only the faces perpendicular to x have flux. At x = 0.1: E = 50, flux in = −50 × 0.01 = −0.5. At x = 0.2: E = 100, flux out = 1.0. Net flux = 0.5 N m² C⁻¹. (b) q = ε₀Φ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² × 0.5 ≈ 4.4 × 10⁻¹² C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Define 'current density'. Is it a scalar or a vector? An electric field E is maintained in a metallic conductor. If n is the number of electrons (mass m, charge −e) per unit volume in the conductor and τ its relaxation time, show that the current density j = αE, where α = (ne²/m)τ.
questions.solution: Current density is the current per unit area normal to the flow; it is a vector. Electrons acquire drift velocity v_d = −eEτ/m. j = −nev_d = (ne²τ/m)E, so α = ne²τ/m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What is a Wheatstone bridge? Obtain the necessary condition under which the Wheatstone bridge is balanced.
questions.solution: Four resistances P, Q, R, S in a closed loop ABCD, with a cell across AC and a galvanometer across BD. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential. Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule to ABDA and BCDB with currents I₁ in P, Q and I₂ in S, R: I₁P = I₂S and I₁Q = I₂R. Dividing, P/Q = S/R.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A proton with kinetic energy 1.3384 × 10⁻¹⁴ J moving horizontally from north to south enters a uniform magnetic field B of 2.0 mT directed eastward. Calculate (a) the speed of the proton (b) the magnitude of acceleration of the proton (c) the radius of the path traced by the proton. [Take q/m for the proton = 1.0 × 10⁸ C/kg]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An inductor, a capacitor and a resistor are connected in series with an ac source v = v_m sin ωt. Derive an expression for the average power dissipated in the circuit. Also obtain the expression for the resonant frequency of the circuit.
questions.solution: i = i_m sin(ωt + φ) with tan φ = (X_C − X_L)/R. p = vi = v_m i_m sin ωt sin(ωt + φ) = (v_m i_m/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt + φ)]. The second term averages to zero, so P = (v_m i_m/2) cos φ = V_rms I_rms cos φ. At resonance X_L = X_C: ωL = 1/(ωC), so ω₀ = 1/√(LC), ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) "The wavelength of an electromagnetic wave is often correlated with the characteristic size of the system that radiates." Give two examples to justify this statement.
(b) (i) Long distance radio broadcasts use short-wave bands. Why? (ii) Optical and radio telescopes are built on the ground, but X-ray astronomy is possible only from satellites orbiting the Earth. Why?
questions.solution: (a) Gamma rays (wavelength about 10⁻¹⁴ m) come from nuclei, which are of that size; visible and UV light (about 10⁻⁷ m) come from atomic transitions in atoms of size about 10⁻¹⁰ m; radio waves come from antennas of size comparable to their wavelength. (b) (i) Short waves are reflected by the ionosphere and return to Earth far away. (ii) The atmosphere is transparent to visible light and radio waves but absorbs X-rays, so X-ray telescopes must be above it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Write the drawbacks of Rutherford's atomic model. How did Bohr remove them? Show that different orbits in Bohr's atom are not equally spaced.
questions.solution: Drawbacks: an accelerating (orbiting) electron should radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus, so atoms would be unstable; and the spectrum would be continuous, not a line spectrum. Bohr postulated stationary orbits where the electron does not radiate, with angular momentum mvr = nh/2π, and that radiation is emitted only when an electron jumps between orbits (hν = E_i − E_f). Since rₙ = n²r₁, the radii are r₁, 4r₁, 9r₁ … and the gaps 3r₁, 5r₁ … increase, so the orbits are not equally spaced.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(a) State any two properties of a nucleus.
(b) Why is the density of a nucleus much more than that of an atom?
(c) Show that the density of nuclear matter is the same for all nuclei.
questions.solution: (a) Its radius R = R₀A^(1/3); its density is about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³, independent of A; it is held together by a strong, short-range nuclear force. (b) Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus, whose volume is about 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's. (c) Mass ≈ Am, volume = (4/3)πR₀³A. Density = Am/((4/3)πR₀³A) = 3m/(4πR₀³), which does not depend on A.

questions.text:

A double-convex lens of power P, with each face having the same radius of curvature, is cut into two equal parts perpendicular to its principal axis. The power of one part of the lens will be :
questions.solution: Each part is plano-convex with one curved surface, so its power is P/2.

A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, with one or both surfaces being spherical. The two plano-convex parts from (ii) are kept in contact with each other, curved faces touching. The power of the combination will be :

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Junction diode as a rectifier: the process of converting an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification, and the device which does this is a rectifier. A p-n junction diode offers a low resistance when forward biased and a high resistance when reverse biased, so it conducts only when forward biased. When an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during the alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only one half cycle of an ac voltage is a half-wave rectifier; one that rectifies both half cycles is a full-wave rectifier.

The root mean square value of an alternating voltage applied to a full-wave rectifier is V₀/√2. Then the root mean square value of the rectified output voltage is :
questions.solution: Full-wave rectification only flips the negative halves, so the mean of v² and hence the rms value is unchanged: V₀/√2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Junction diode as a rectifier: the process of converting an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification, and the device which does this is a rectifier. A p-n junction diode offers a low resistance when forward biased and a high resistance when reverse biased, so it conducts only when forward biased. When an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during the alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only one half cycle of an ac voltage is a half-wave rectifier; one that rectifies both half cycles is a full-wave rectifier.

In a full-wave rectifier, the current in each of the diodes flows for :
options: Complete cycle of the input signal
Half cycle of the input signal
Less than half cycle of the input signal
Only for the positive half cycle of the input signal
questions.solution: Each diode conducts during alternate half cycles.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Junction diode as a rectifier: the process of converting an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification, and the device which does this is a rectifier. A p-n junction diode offers a low resistance when forward biased and a high resistance when reverse biased, so it conducts only when forward biased. When an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during the alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only one half cycle of an ac voltage is a half-wave rectifier; one that rectifies both half cycles is a full-wave rectifier.

In a full-wave rectifier :
options: Both diodes are forward biased at the same time.
Both diodes are reverse biased at the same time.
One is forward biased and the other is reverse biased at the same time.
Both are forward biased in the first half of the cycle and reverse biased in the second half of the cycle.
questions.solution: At any instant one diode conducts and the other is reverse biased.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
Junction diode as a rectifier: the process of converting an ac voltage into a dc voltage is called rectification, and the device which does this is a rectifier. A p-n junction diode offers a low resistance when forward biased and a high resistance when reverse biased, so it conducts only when forward biased. When an ac voltage is applied across a p-n junction, it conducts only during the alternate half cycles for which it is forward biased. A rectifier which rectifies only one half cycle of an ac voltage is a half-wave rectifier; one that rectifies both half cycles is a full-wave rectifier.

An alternating voltage of frequency 50 Hz is applied to a half-wave rectifier. Then the ripple frequency of the output will be :
questions.solution: A half-wave rectifier gives one output pulse per input cycle, so the ripple frequency equals the input frequency, 50 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Derive an expression for the potential energy of an electric dipole p in an external uniform electric field E. When is the potential energy of the dipole (1) maximum, and (2) minimum?
(ii) An electric dipole consists of point charges −1.0 pC and +1.0 pC located at (0, 0) and (3 mm, 4 mm) respectively in the x-y plane. An electric field E = (1000 V/m) î is switched on in the region. Find the torque τ acting on the dipole.
questions.solution: (i) The torque on the dipole is pE sin θ. Work done in rotating it from θ₀ to θ: W = ∫ pE sin θ dθ = pE(cos θ₀ − cos θ). Taking U = 0 at θ₀ = 90°, U = −pE cos θ = −p · E. (1) Maximum (+pE) at θ = 180° (antiparallel, unstable equilibrium); (2) minimum (−pE) at θ = 0° (parallel, stable equilibrium). (ii) p = q × (3 î + 4 ĵ) mm = 10⁻¹² × (3 × 10⁻³ î + 4 × 10⁻³ ĵ) C m. τ = p × E = 10⁻¹⁵ (3 î + 4 ĵ) × 1000 î = 4 × 10⁻¹² (ĵ × î) = −4 × 10⁻¹² k̂ N m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) An electric dipole (dipole moment p = p î), consisting of charges −q and q separated by distance 2a, is placed along the x-axis with its centre at the origin. Show that the potential V due to this dipole at a point x (x ≫ a) is equal to (1/4πε₀)(p · î)/x².
(ii) Two isolated metallic spheres S₁ and S₂ of radii 1 cm and 3 cm respectively are charged such that both have the same charge density (2/π) × 10⁻⁹ C/m². They are placed far away from each other and connected by a thin wire. Calculate the new charge on sphere S₁.
questions.solution: (i) +q is at x = a and −q at x = −a. V = kq[1/(x − a) − 1/(x + a)] = kq(2a)/(x² − a²) ≈ k(2aq)/x² = (1/4πε₀)(p · î)/x² for x ≫ a. (ii) q = σ4πr²: q₁ = (2/π)10⁻⁹ × 4π × 10⁻⁴ = 8 × 10⁻¹³ C, q₂ = 9q₁ = 7.2 × 10⁻¹² C; total 8 × 10⁻¹² C. Connected, they share charge in the ratio of radii (equal potentials): q₁′ = 8 × 10⁻¹² × 1/4 = 2 × 10⁻¹² C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) A resistor and a capacitor are connected in series to an ac source v = v_m sin ωt. Derive an expression for the impedance of the circuit.
(ii) When does an inductor act as a conductor in a circuit? Give reason for it.
(iii) An electric lamp is designed to operate at 110 V dc and 11 A current. If the lamp is operated on a 220 V, 50 Hz ac source with a coil in series, find the inductance of the coil.
questions.solution: (i) The same current flows through both; V_R = iR is in phase with i and V_C = iX_C lags it by 90°. From the phasor diagram V² = V_R² + V_C², so v_m = i_m√(R² + X_C²) and Z = √(R² + 1/(ω²C²)). (ii) In a dc circuit (in steady state), since X_L = ωL = 0 at zero frequency, the inductor offers no reactance and acts as a plain conductor. (iii) R = 110/11 = 10 Ω. Z = 220/11 = 20 Ω, so X_L = √(400 − 100) = 10√3 Ω. L = X_L/(2π × 50) = 10√3/(100π) ≈ 0.055 H.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) Draw a labelled diagram of a step-up transformer and describe its working principle. Explain any three causes of energy losses in a real transformer.
(ii) A step-up transformer converts a low voltage into a high voltage. Does it violate the principle of conservation of energy? Explain.
(iii) A step-up transformer has 200 and 3000 turns in its primary and secondary coils respectively. The input voltage given to the primary coil is 90 V. Calculate (1) the output voltage across the secondary coil (2) the current in the primary coil if the current in the secondary coil is 2.0 A.
questions.solution: (i) Primary and secondary coils (secondary with more turns) on a laminated soft iron core; it works by mutual induction. Losses: flux leakage, copper (I²R) loss in the windings, eddy-current loss in the core (reduced by lamination), hysteresis loss. (ii) No. Voltage increases but current decreases in the same ratio, so power VI is (ideally) unchanged. (iii) (1) Vₛ = 90 × 3000/200 = 1350 V. (2) Iₚ = IₛNₛ/Nₚ = 2 × 15 = 30 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) A ray of light passes through a triangular prism. Show graphically how the angle of deviation varies with the angle of incidence. Hence define the angle of minimum deviation.
(ii) A ray of light is incident normally on a refracting face of a prism of prism angle A and suffers a deviation of angle δ. Prove that the refractive index n of the material of the prism is given by n = sin(A + δ)/sin A.
(iii) The refractive index of the material of a prism is √2. If the refracting angle of the prism is 60°, find (1) the angle of minimum deviation, and (2) the angle of incidence.
questions.solution: (i) As i increases, δ first decreases, reaches a minimum δₘ and then increases (a U-shaped curve). δₘ is the smallest deviation, when the ray passes symmetrically (i = e, r₁ = r₂). (ii) Normal incidence: r₁ = 0, so r₂ = A. Deviation δ = e − A, so e = A + δ. At the second face n sin A = sin e, giving n = sin(A + δ)/sin A. (iii) n = sin((A + δₘ)/2)/sin(A/2): √2 × ½ = sin((60° + δₘ)/2), so (60° + δₘ)/2 = 45° and δₘ = 30°. (2) i = (A + δₘ)/2 = 45°.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text:
(i) State Huygens' principle. A plane wave is incident at an angle i on a reflecting surface. Construct the corresponding reflected wavefront. Using this diagram, prove that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence.
(ii) What are coherent sources of light? Can two independent sodium lamps act like coherent sources? Explain.
(iii) A beam of light consisting of a known wavelength 520 nm and an unknown wavelength λ, used in Young's double slit experiment, produces two interference patterns such that the fourth bright fringe of the unknown wavelength coincides with the fifth bright fringe of the known wavelength. Find the value of λ.
questions.solution: (i) Every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; the new wavefront is the forward envelope of these wavelets. Let wavefront AB meet the mirror at A. While the wave from B travels BC = vt to the mirror, the wavelet from A grows to radius AE = vt. The reflected wavefront is CE. Triangles ABC and CEA are congruent (common AC, BC = AE, right angles at B and E), so ∠i = ∠r. (ii) Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference. No: in two independent lamps atoms emit randomly, so the phase difference changes rapidly. (iii) 4λD/d = 5 × 520 D/d, so λ = 650 nm.
